newsitem.title: USA: Huge China LPG demand to lift import prices.
newsitem.headline: Huge China LPG demand to lift import prices.

text.p: A widening gap between supply and demand in China for liquefied petroleum gas products (LPGs) is expected to increase the country's reliance on imports and pressure up prices for cargoes, mainly from the Middle East, analysts said Monday.

Already the third largest importer of LPGs in the Asia-Pacific region, China is expected to pull even greater volumes off the international market in the next few years to satisfy its growing economy.
"Over the next ten years, China has the potential to become a huge consumer of LPG," said the Washington-based Energy Security Analysts Inc (ESAI).
Since the early 1990s, consumption rates in China have grown by more than 20 percent a year, while production has increased only nine percent.
"The gap between supply and demand has been widening and this trend is expected to continue over the next ten years," said ESAI in its report, ChinaWatch.

LPG is primarily used in China as a fuel for cooking, heating and cooling for domestic, commercial and industrial use. About 15 percent of total consumption is used as feedstock by petrochemical companies.

In 1996, LPG imports to China rose by more than 50 percent to more than 100,000 barrels per day, making China the third largest LPG importer in the Asia-Pacific region following Japan and South Korea.
Due to the increase, more than half of China's LPG supply now comes from foreign sources -- increasingly from Saudi Arabia, the world's largest LPG exporter.
"This increase in demand from China could definitely have an upward pressure on prices on supply from the Middle East," said ESAI analyst Masa Koyama.

The level of imports in 1997 is not expected to increase as dramatically as last year because of inadequate storage. But once facilities come on line starting in 1998, China could be receiving as much as 180,000 bpd by 2000, said ESAI.
The analysts forecast imports reaching 300,000 bpd by 2005.
"These volumes will need to be supplied by the world market and profitable opportunities will arise for those able to provide this increasingly important fuel," said the ChinaWatch report.
